subject: rider
name: Mounting & Dismounting
summary: Safely checking tack, mounting smoothly from a mounting block or ground, settling into the saddle, and dismounting cleanly.
purpose: Protects the horse's back and ensures the rider starts and finishes every ride safely and in control.
safety: Check saddle stability, girth/cinch snugness, bridle/halter security, and stirrup length before mounting—and re-check girth snugness again after walking a few steps.
Always use a stable mounting block or raised bank whenever available to reduce twisting torque on the horse's spine and saddle tree.

introductory.overview: Completing a pre-mount safety and readiness check, mounting smoothly without pulling on the cantle or mouth, adjusting tack safely, and dismounting cleanly.

components.title: Pre-mount horse and tack check
components.description: Verifying girth/cinch comfort, clean stitching, stirrup security, and calm horse attention at the mounting block before putting weight in a stirrup.

components.title: Elastic mount, post-mount check, and dismount
components.description: Holding light non-pulling rein feel over the crest, springing gently without kicking the rump or dropping heavily onto the back, adjusting stirrups and girth calmly after walking forward a few strides, and sliding smoothly clear on dismount without snagging spurs or boots.

introductory.learning: Mounts and dismounts a quiet horse with supervision holding the horse, prompting girth checks, or smoothing the landing in the saddle.
introductory.proficient: Independently completes a pre-mount tack and horse-readiness check, mounts cleanly from a block without twisting the saddle or thumping the horse's back, re-checks girth comfort calmly, and dismounts smoothly with clear balance.

exercises.title: Pre-Mount Check and Weight-Centered Entry
exercises.summary: Before putting a foot in the stirrup, inspect girth or cinch snugness, bridle fit, and arena clearance. Step up smoothly from a stable mounting block or raised bank, hovering briefly over your base rather than pulling sideways on the cantle or mouth, and lower yourself lightly into the saddle.
exercises.whatToNotice: Notice whether the saddle twists sideways as you rise—engaging your core over the block rather than hauling down with one hand protects both saddle tree and equine spine.

exercises.title: Settled Pause, Girth Re-Check, and Clean Dismount
exercises.summary: After settling into the saddle, reward a peaceful pause for several seconds before asking the horse forward, walk a short distance and re-check girth snugness safely, and finish rides with a quiet halt and smooth step-down free of caught clothing or stirrups.
exercises.whatToNotice: Check whether you drop straight into forward motion out of habit—giving your horse a relaxed breath after mounting prevents rush-off patterns.

commonDifficulties.issue: Horse stepping forward as your toe touches the stirrup
commonDifficulties.guidance: Anticipating an instant walk cue teaches moving off mid-mount. Pause calmly with soft reins before stepping up, reward quiet standing, and only ask for walk once fully settled.

commonDifficulties.issue: Hitting the saddle heavily on landing
commonDifficulties.guidance: Dropping abruptly strains the horse’s thoracic back. Use a taller block whenever available and bend knees slightly to absorb landing weight like stepping onto thin ice.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Every ride starts on the mounting block—pause long enough after landing for your horse to relax before asking for a step.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Repeated sidestepping or ear pinning at the block warrants checking girth comfort, saddle pinching, and back tenderness rather than assuming impatience.

subject: rider
name: Independent Seat, Position & Balance
summary: Maintaining centered rider alignment, shock-absorbing balance, and hand independence while following the horse's motion across disciplines.
purpose: Protects the horse's back and mouth while allowing the rider to move harmoniously and adapt safely across varied horses, saddles, and riding contexts.
safety: Keep balance centered over your pelvis, legs, and feet rather than using the reins as a handle or support strap.

Respect legitimate discipline- and conformation-appropriate postures—adjusting stirrup length, saddle fit, or seat style (full seat, light seat, two-point) for both rider symmetry and equine back comfort.
Address tension, knee gripping, or persistent rider crookedness early so physical strain does not spill into equine bracing or soreness.

introductory.overview: Developing calm baseline alignment, relaxing knee or hip gripping, following quiet walk and early trot/jog motion without relying on the reins for balance, and noticing obvious collapse or tension.

components.title: Alignment and relaxed base
components.description: Organizing an upright, stackable posture suited to your tack and discipline (functional ear–shoulder–hip–heel balance without rigid arching or slumped collapse) while allowing ankles, knees, and hips to stay unlocked.

components.title: Following motion without rein dependence
components.description: Allowing the pelvis to absorb calm walk and introductory trot/jog motion cleanly while resting hands comfortably on light contact, loose rein, or gentle neck/grab-strap support without pulling on the horse's mouth for stability.

components.title: Common mistakes and horse back comfort
components.description: Common mistakes include tipping ahead on starts, bracing feet forward onto the cantle, locking knees, or holding breath. Notice how heavy bouncing or rigid gripping restricts the horse's back.

introductory.learning: Practices balanced posture at walk and early trot/jog with occasional slumping, knee gripping, tense breathing, or brief reliance on saddle horn, mane, or reins when stride speed changes.
introductory.proficient: Independently organizes centered, discipline-appropriate alignment at walk and early trot or jog, absorbs movement smoothly without depending on the reins for balance, and notices and corrects obvious posture collapse or tension.

intermediate.overview: Maintaining independent balance across comfortable gaits, curves, and routine transitions across legitimate riding positions while identifying and self-correcting personal asymmetry.

components.title: Independent balance across transitions and positions
components.description: Moving smoothly between relaxed deep seat, working upright posture, and balanced light/two-point positions (as appropriate to saddle and discipline) through walk, trot/jog, canter/lope, turns, and transitions without catching on the reins.

components.title: Recognizing and addressing personal asymmetry
components.description: Noticing personal habits—such as weighting one seat bone more heavily, collapsing a waist/hip, stiffening one knee, or turning shoulders unequally—and resetting straightness purposefully in both directions.

components.title: Recovering rhythm without grabbing
components.description: Adjusting calmly if a stirrup slips slightly, footing varies, or a stride lengthens unexpectedly without locking joints or pulling backward.

intermediate.learning: Maintains balanced alignment on familiar tracks while occasionally dropping onto one hip in corners, pitching slightly during transitions, or needing reminders to spot side-to-side asymmetry.
intermediate.proficient: Independently sustains non-rein-dependent balance across comfortable gaits, turns, transitions, and legitimate seat positions (such as full or light seat), identifies and self-corrects left/right rider asymmetry, and recovers smoothly from minor balance shifts.

advanced.overview: Sustaining an elastic, shock-absorbing, adaptive independent seat across diverse horses, within-gait changes, varied terrain, and demanding movements while keeping hands unaffected and responsive.

components.title: Dynamic adaptability across horses and terrain
components.description: Adapting balance, core tone, and shock absorption instantaneously across horses of varied gaits, conformation, ages, or builds—as well as uneven outdoor grades, transitions, and lateral work—across riding disciplines.

components.title: Quiet hand independence under complex aids
components.description: Applying independent seat, weight, and leg coordination without unintentionally pulling on the reins, leaning out of balance, or stiffening breathing during energetic strides or sudden adjustments.

components.title: Subtle symmetry and equine welfare awareness
components.description: Detecting minor personal stiffness or saddle imbalance early before it loads one side of the horse's spine unfairly, choosing fair equipment or position adjustments to support relaxed movement.

advanced.learning: Rides diverse tasks with generally sound balance while working to refine subtle asymmetry, elastic timing on large movers, or complete hand quietness during unexpected shifts.
advanced.proficient: Independently adapts an elastic, well-aligned, shock-absorbing seat across varied horses, gaits, movements, and terrain—maintaining steady hand independence, proactively correcting subtle asymmetry, and supporting equine back comfort across disciplines.

exercises.title: Breathe, Follow, and Ride Free of the Reins
exercises.summary: At a steady walk on a quiet partner, look smoothly ahead, exhale slowly, and let hips, knees, and ankles unlock so your seat bones follow each hind step. Keep reins soft—or rest lightly near mane or a neck strap—without steady-holding the mouth to balance your torso.
exercises.whatToNotice: Do your hands float softly with the stride while your elbows absorb motion, or do knees clamp, toes brace forward, and shoulders tip when pace varies?

exercises.title: Smooth Shifts Between Full and Light Seat
exercises.summary: Starting on straight lines at walk before adding faster gaits when secure, fold smoothly over ankles and knees into a balanced light or two-point position for a few strides, then settle gently back into the saddle without thumping the back or grabbing the reins.
exercises.whatToNotice: Feel left-to-right symmetry across both stirrups and legs in both directions, noticing if one hip collapses or one knee grips harder during transitions.

commonDifficulties.issue: Gripping with the knees or calves to feel steady
commonDifficulties.guidance: Clamping upward lifts your balance off the horse's center and stiffens the horse's back. Drop your breath, soften thigh tension downward, and work at an easier pace until ease returns.

commonDifficulties.issue: Steadying yourself with the reins in transitions
commonDifficulties.guidance: Even brief backward catches tense the horse's jaw and neck. Cue transitions earlier with breath and posture, and keep a simple neck strap handy while building stability.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Real security lives over your own pelvis and feet; hands stay light only when they are never asked to rescue your balance.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Persistent rider crookedness, heavy bouncing, or a slipping saddle puts uneven strain on the horse's spine—check stirrup symmetry, saddle fit, and early signs of back tension promptly.

subject: rider
name: Emergency Situations & Recovery
summary: Using situational awareness, balance recovery, early de-escalation, and sound risk judgment to manage unexpected mounted situations safely.
purpose: Helps riders prevent avoidable accidents early and choose calm, context-appropriate safety responses rather than reacting in panic or relying blindly on one risky habit.
safety: Prioritize prevention first through arena/trail awareness, tack checks, sensible footing/spacing choices, and ending or simplifying a task before stress escalates.

No single emergency technique—including an emergency dismount or a one-rein stop—is appropriate or safe in every situation; consider speed, balance, terrain, obstacles, footing traction, and horse sensitivity before acting.
Never hesitate to pause, step off safely when halted or safe to do so, or call on an instructor, ground person, or equine professional whenever risk exceeds skill or control.

introductory.overview: Practicing situational awareness before problems escalate, staying centered during mild unexpected movement, recovering lost reins or stirrups calmly, and knowing when and how to seek assistance.

components.title: Situational awareness and early prevention
components.description: Scanning surroundings for footing hazards, close herd/arena traffic, shifting saddles, or early equine tension (braced neck, startled eyes, distracted tail) so you can slow down, widen space, or pause early.

components.title: Maintaining balance during mild surprises
components.description: Exhaling, softening down into your base without pulling back on the mouth, steadying calmly on mane/saddle/neck if needed during a small spook, trip, or sudden step, and quietly gathering dropped reins or lost stirrups without panicking.

components.title: Safe pauses, controlled dismounts, and seeking help
components.description: Recognizing when a situation warrants stopping calmly in clear space, waiting for assistance, or completing a controlled, stationary dismount clear of obstacles rather than forcing through rising anxiety.

introductory.learning: Practices noticing triggers and recovering reins or stirrups calmly on quiet horses while occasionally freezing, holding breath, or needing coaching to spot tension early or decide when to ask for help.
introductory.proficient: Independently maintains practical situational awareness in familiar settings, takes calm preventive steps when tension or hazards appear, keeps centered balance during mild unexpected steps or lost stirrups/reins, and recognizes promptly when to stop, dismount safely, or request assistance.

intermediate.overview: Judging dynamic hazards early in varied settings, staying balanced through sudden shies, stumbles, or surges, and selecting safe, circumstance-appropriate responses rather than applying a fixed rule blindly.

components.title: Early de-escalation and environmental risk assessment
components.description: Reading rising equine arousal, herd contagion, loose hardware, or slick/steep terrain well ahead of escalation—proactively downgrading pace, turning onto open footing, or stopping a ride safely before control breaks down.

components.title: Composed balance during unexpected motion
components.description: Following sudden shies, stumbles, buck/hop shifts, or hurried departures with elastic hips and breath rather than curling forward, snatching both reins tight, or losing emotional composure.

components.title: Selecting context-appropriate safety responses
components.description: Choosing responses matched cleanly to space, footing, horse training, and speed—for instance softening breath and redirecting forward attention on a calm curving path where clear ground allows, using smooth progressive down-transitions, or waiting to dismount only where ground and speed permit (knowing why emergency dismounts or sharp one-rein stops can injure horse or rider on slick turf, narrow trails, or high speed) and calling qualified help when warranted.

intermediate.learning: Handles mild unexpected motion in busier or open settings while occasionally pulling reflexively when startled or hesitating over which preventive or recovery choice best fits the terrain and space.
intermediate.proficient: Independently anticipates developing risks early across varied environments, stays centered and calm through unexpected horse movements or minor tack disruptions, chooses safe context-appropriate de-escalation or recovery actions without forcing one universal maneuver, and seeks support wisely whenever conditions demand it.

exercises.title: Preventive Scanning and Recovering Lost Tack at Walk
exercises.summary: At a relaxed walk in an enclosed arena on a quiet partner, scan ahead for footing shifts or barn activity before tension builds. While staying centered and upright, practice dropping and smoothly catching one stirrup or gathering a dropped rein without tipping forward or grabbing the mouth.
exercises.whatToNotice: Notice whether shoulders hunch and your chin drops when retrieving a stirrup—staying tall over your pelvis keeps balance steady without looking down.

exercises.title: Planned De-Escalation and Terrain Judgment Walk-Through
exercises.summary: Before riding out or in lively venues, rehearse calm options: slowing pace before narrow gaps, turning onto larger open circles to restore thinking, or halting cleanly to step off on flat footing if worry stacks. Match responses to terrain, speed, and horse readiness rather than applying one fixed rule.
exercises.whatToNotice: Ask yourself whether you spot early tension—shortened strides, held breath, locked neck—early enough to redirect calmly while options stay safe.

commonDifficulties.issue: Freezing with tightened thighs and pulled-back hands during a mild startle
commonDifficulties.guidance: Clamping legs and stiffening reins often drives faster flight. Focus on exhaling, sitting deep over balanced ankles, widening eyes forward, and steering softly onto an open curve once safe.

commonDifficulties.issue: Assuming one emergency habit works on every surface or horse
commonDifficulties.guidance: Abrupt lateral flexing on slick hills or leaping off at speed creates severe fall hazards. Adjust choices thoughtfully to traction, obstacles, speed, and horse balance.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Good emergency horsemanship rarely looks dramatic—it prevents 90% of crises ten strides before they erupt.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Never deliberately induce spooks, bolting, or extreme reactions to rehearse emergencies; practice calm recovery only within settled paces and step off safely when risk exceeds readiness.

subject: rider
name: Walk
summary: Following the horse's four-beat walk in balance while maintaining calm direction, adjustable stride length, and clean halts.
purpose: Establishes independent rider balance, supple hips, quiet hands, and calm communication before faster gaits.
safety: Keep heels relaxed and hands independent of balance so you never brace on the horse's mouth.
Maintain safe spacing from other horses.

introductory.overview: Maintaining a balanced, relaxed seat at walk, asking smoothly for walk, and halting safely without bracing on the reins.

components.title: Following the four-beat motion
components.description: Allowing the pelvis to move naturally with the horse's alternating four-beat stride and keeping hands elastic so the horse's head and neck can nod freely. Common mistake: stiffening the lower back or fixing the hands, which restricts the walk and causes tension.

components.title: Basic walk starts and halts
components.description: Using light seat, leg, and voice cues to ask for walk and returning calmly to halt without pulling abruptly.

introductory.learning: Walks on a quiet horse with occasional stiffness, gripping, or reliance on the reins for balance.
introductory.proficient: Independently asks for walk, follows the four-beat motion comfortably with balanced posture and soft, non-restrictive reins (whether on light contact or a loose rein), and returns calmly to halt.

intermediate.overview: Influencing walk energy, stride length (active working walk vs. relaxed free walk), and straightness without disturbing four-beat purity.

components.title: Working walk vs. free walk
components.description: Adjusting between an active, marching working walk and a long, relaxed free walk where the horse stretches forward and down. Why it matters: preserves back suppleness and tests whether the horse stays rhythmic without constant rein hold.

components.title: Preserving pure four-beat rhythm
components.description: Common mistake: pushing too hard with the legs against tight hands, which causes the horse to hurry into a tight two-beat lateral pace (ambling/pacing) or jog. Welfare note: a restricted neck creates tension through the poll and back.

intermediate.learning: Practices adjusting walk stride length and energy with intermittent loss of four-beat rhythm or hurried steps.
intermediate.proficient: Independently rides an active, rhythmic four-beat walk, lengthens into relaxed free walk and shortens smoothly back to working walk without breaking gait or losing purity.

exercises.title: Following Four-Beat Motion With Soft Hands
exercises.summary: Ride straight lines and wide curves at walk on light contact or a relaxed draped rein, allowing your hips to sway gently side-to-side and forward with each stride while shoulders stay upright and relaxed. Ask for quiet halts with a soft breath and steady seat before taking gentle feel on the reins.
exercises.whatToNotice: Check whether your hands stay elastic enough for the horse’s head and neck to nod naturally at each walk beat—stiff elbows quickly turn four clean beats into a choppy jog.

exercises.title: Alternating Free Walk Stretch and Working Walk
exercises.summary: Along an open straight track, invite a generous free walk where the horse reaches its head forward and down over a loose or softly lengthening rein for several strides, then gently re-gather seat focus and balanced contact or drape back into an active working walk without hurrying.
exercises.whatToNotice: Observe whether stride length and reach change through your seat and breathing while the four-beat footfall cadence remains smooth and unhurried.

commonDifficulties.issue: Pushing faster with constant leg clamping in walk
commonDifficulties.guidance: Nagging with calves deadens sensitivity and hollows the back. Ask crisply once for lively swing, then let legs hang quietly along the sides so movement flows freely.

commonDifficulties.issue: Locking elbows during free walk stretch
commonDifficulties.guidance: Letting fingers open smoothly forward lets the horse stretch down without pulling you ahead out of balance.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: The walk tells the truth about both horse relaxation and hand elasticity—respect its natural nod.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Fixing a horse’s head tightly or rushing walk rhythm quickly creates poll, back, and lateral pacing tension; preserve neck freedom across all transitions.

subject: rider
name: Trot
summary: Riding the symmetrical two-beat trot or jog in balance—progressing from balanced rising trot to diagonal control and refined, independent sitting trot.
purpose: Builds rider core stability, rhythm awareness, diagonal coordination, and supple shock absorption across a two-beat gait.
safety: Keep balance centered over your own seat and ankles rather than gripping upward with knees or catching yourself on the horse's mouth.
Adjust rising or sitting posture sensibly to the horse's stride length and back comfort—check saddle fit or soreness if the horse repeatedly hollows or rushes.

introductory.overview: Riding a steady two-beat trot or jog comfortably in balance—whether rising (posting) trot or relaxed sitting jog—without hanging on the reins, and returning calmly to walk.

components.title: Balanced rising trot or relaxed sitting jog
components.description: Moving with the horse's two-beat lift (rising and lowering softly in posting trot, or absorbing gentle stride motion through supple hips in a slow sitting jog) without double-bouncing, slamming the back, or tightening knees.

components.title: Independent hands and common mistakes
components.description: Keeping elbows elastic so hands stay steady while the body rides the two-beat rhythm. Common mistakes: using the reins to pull yourself upright or leaning stiffly ahead of the motion.

introductory.learning: Trots or jogs short stretches with occasional double-bouncing, stiff lower back, or reliance on a grab strap or reins for balance.
introductory.proficient: Independently transitions into trot or jog, maintains balanced rhythm in either rising trot (regardless of diagonal) or a relaxed sitting jog for sustained stretches without pulling on the reins, and returns calmly to walk.

intermediate.overview: Coordinating rising and sitting trot cleanly across disciplines, identifying diagonals accurately, and deliberately changing posting diagonals smoothly.

components.title: Diagonal feel and clean changes
components.description: Feeling which outside shoulder moves forward as your hips rise without staring down at the horse's knees, and sitting (or standing) two beats smoothly to switch diagonals on turns or straight lines.

components.title: Balanced sitting trot endurance
components.description: Allowing lumbar joints, hips, and ankles to move elastically in a working sitting trot or active jog without pounding the saddle or blocking forward motion.

intermediate.learning: Rides sitting and rising trot and changes diagonals with intermittent stiffness, double-beats on transitions, or glancing down to check alignment.
intermediate.proficient: Independently demonstrates both balanced sitting trot and rising trot, accurately recognizes by feel and deliberately changes posting diagonals in both directions, and maintains steady tempo with quiet hands.

advanced.overview: Maintaining an independent, shock-absorbing sitting trot through demanding figures, within-gait changes, and lateral work without blocking the horse's back.

components.title: Independent seat and hand coordination
components.description: Keeping deep supple hip absorption and quiet, unaffected hands while coordinating precise weight, leg, and rein cues through turns, medium/lengthened strides, direct transitions, and lateral movements.

advanced.learning: Maintains sitting trot in simple work with occasional hip stiffening, bouncing during lengthenings, or hand movement when giving stronger aids.
advanced.proficient: Independently sustains a supple, shock-absorbing sitting trot through applicable movements—including transitions, circles, within-gait adjustments, and lateral work—using quiet, non-blocking aids that let the horse's back swing freely.

exercises.title: Balanced Rising Trot or Relaxed Sitting Jog
exercises.summary: From an active walk on large tracks, ride brief comfortable stretches of two-beat trot—either rising (posting) softly with the horse’s motion or riding a relaxed sitting jog in Western/balanced setups—letting the stride bounce you gently rather than pulling forward on the reins, then return smoothly to walk.
exercises.whatToNotice: Feel whether knees stay heavy and soft over balanced ankles so your hands never bob up and down against the mouth.

exercises.title: Diagonal Awareness and Smooth Tempo Shifts
exercises.summary: When posting on wide curves or circles, feel or glance briefly down at the outside shoulder to confirm your rising diagonal matches the curve, practice changing diagonals smoothly via one extra sit-beat across figure changes, and explore smooth rising-to-sitting transitions suited to the horse’s readiness.
exercises.whatToNotice: Notice whether you sense diagonal rhythm from the ribcage underneath you without tipping shoulders forward when glancing down.

commonDifficulties.issue: Standing high out of the saddle or collapsing onto the cantle
commonDifficulties.guidance: Over-posting strains balance and drops weight hard on the back. Let the horse lift your hips gently just above the saddle and hover softly down.

commonDifficulties.issue: Bouncing stiffly in sitting trot
commonDifficulties.guidance: Gripping thighs locks your lower back. Keep sitting periods brief, focus on slow exhales, and ensure the horse’s back is warm and swinging cleanly before asking more.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Post only as high as the horse’s stride lifts you; quiet posting protects their back far better than exaggerated athletics.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Vary posting diagonals evenly between sessions, shorten sitting work for stiff or green backs, and pause to check saddle fit or soreness if rhythmic unevenness appears.

subject: rider
name: Canter
summary: Preparing, following, and regulating the three-beat canter or lope with balance, rhythm, clear timing, lead feel, simple lead changes, and within-gait adjustability—prioritizing horse comfort and relaxation across disciplines.
purpose: Develops hip suppleness, rhythmic core stability, accurate aid timing, and adaptable three-beat balance without equating speed or specialized maneuvers with horsemanship.
safety: Establish calm walk and trot control, clear steering, and safe spacing from other horses or hazards before cantering.
Evaluate footing, traction, slope, and turn radius before asking for canter; avoid tight turns or unbalanced departures on slick, deep, or rocky ground.
Treat repeated rushing, cross-cantering, hollowing, or one-sided lead resistance as important welfare feedback—slow down and assess saddle fit, soreness, conditioning, footing, or your own alignment.

introductory.overview: Preparing a calm depart from walk or trot, following the forward three-beat motion comfortably in a full or light/two-point seat (on light contact or a loose rein), and returning smoothly to trot or walk. Correct lead selection is not required.

components.title: Calm preparation vs. running the trot
components.description: Preparing a steady walk or balanced trot before asking lightly, rather than speeding up the trot until the horse trips or rushes into canter.

components.title: Following 3-beat feel and non-restrictive balance
components.description: Letting hips sweep cleanly with the stride in either full seat or light/two-point seat without gripping knees or balancing off the horse's mouth.

components.title: Controlled returns
components.description: Exhaling, stabilizing the core quietly, and gliding smoothly down to trot or walk while space remains clear.

introductory.learning: Departs into canter for short stretches with guidance; seat, hands, or breathing occasionally brace during transitions, or trot speeds up beforehand.
introductory.proficient: Independently prepares a balanced walk or trot, asks calmly for canter, follows the three-beat motion comfortably in full or light seat without balancing off the reins, steers simple lines/curves, and makes a controlled downward transition. Correct lead selection is not required at this level.

intermediate.overview: Preparing requested left and right leads from walk or trot, feeling which lead the horse is on without looking down, balancing curves and turns smoothly, riding calm simple lead changes, and handling wrong leads constructively.

components.title: Lead feel and anatomy without looking down
components.description: Understanding that the lead leg advances farther and feeling the corresponding forward swing of your hip/shoulder silently rather than staring down at the horse's shoulder.

components.title: Turns, generous curves, and simple lead changes
components.description: Aligning shoulders and weight smoothly around turns and generous circles or sweeping curves without leaning inward; riding calm simple lead changes through walk or trot.

components.title: Constructive adjustment and welfare
components.description: Recognizing an unintended wrong lead or disunited canter promptly, transitioning calmly back to rebalance instead of yanking, and checking comfort or rider bias if one lead is consistently difficult.

intermediate.learning: Selects leads, balances curves, and practices simple lead changes with occasional wrong-lead departs, looking down to check, leaning inward, or hurried change transitions.
intermediate.proficient: Independently prepares and asks for left and right leads from walk or trot, identifies leads by feel, maintains steady three-beat balance through turns and generous curves on light contact or a loose rein, performs clean simple lead changes, and transitions calmly to rebalance unintended or disunited leads.

advanced.overview: Refined fundamental canter mastery: regulating stride length and balance cleanly within the three-beat gait (without rushing), staying poised and aligned across varied lines, terrain, or transitions suited to the horse, and adapting thoughtfully for equine welfare. Counter-canter and flying lead changes are separate optional skills.

components.title: Within-gait adjustability (speed is not skill)
components.description: Lengthening and shortening canter stride smoothly through seat, core tone, and release timing while keeping calm three-beat rhythm rather than flattening/accelerating or pulling continuously.

components.title: Uphill balance, timing, and adaptability
components.description: Delivering subtle, clear aids tailored to stride rhythm across varied lines, curves, terrain, or transitions appropriate to the horse's build and discipline—adapting contact, posture, and pace thoughtfully.

components.title: Observing subtle fatigue or tension
components.description: Reading stiffening through the back, hurried breathing, or late hind engagement early so demands remain humane and productive.

advanced.learning: Practices within-gait lengthenings/shortenings and varied balanced canter work with intermittent flattening, bracing on the reins, crookedness, or late posture adjustments.
advanced.proficient: Independently rides a relaxed, balanced three-beat canter or lope with clear within-gait stride adjustability (lengthening and shortening without rushing), straight alignment, subtle aid timing across varied lines and transitions suited to the horse and footing, and attentive welfare-based adaptation.

exercises.title: Calm Depart Preparation and Supple Following Seat
exercises.summary: Once walk and trot balance feel steady with open arena spacing, prepare a smooth canter depart from a balanced trot or energetic walk corner in either a deep following seat or light/two-point position—without gripping the reins—and glide calmly back down to trot or walk after a relaxed curve.
exercises.whatToNotice: Notice whether you brace your hips backward or tip shoulders steeply inward on the depart; letting your lower back swing smoothly with the stride keeps hands still.

exercises.title: Lead Feel, Curves, and Calm Simple Lead Changes
exercises.summary: On generous curves in both directions, cue the requested inside lead clearly, confirm by body symmetry and shoulder reach rather than staring straight down, ride balanced large circles, and practice calm simple lead changes through walk or trot across direction changes.
exercises.whatToNotice: Check whether mild inside leg and outside rib balance invite the requested lead cleanly, and verify your response when a wrong lead happens stays patient rather than startled.

commonDifficulties.issue: Throwing your upper body forward to chase the depart
commonDifficulties.guidance: Lunging forward loads the horse’s forehand and triggers hurried running trot instead of canter. Sit tall, soften your breath, and ride cleanly through a balanced curve.

commonDifficulties.issue: Panicking or jerking the reins when the wrong lead occurs
commonDifficulties.guidance: Sharp corrections punish communication. Quietly return to trot or walk, rebalance your own hips and straightness, and ask again cleanly.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: A good canter depart is born in the three balanced strides before you ever touch with your outside leg.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Match canter footing, circle size, and duration to horse fitness; treat chronic cross-cantering, rushing, or one-sided lead struggles as feedback to assess saddle fit and comfort.

subject: rider
name: Counter-Canter
summary: Intentionally riding balanced, relaxed canter or lope on the outside lead through straight lines, shallow loops, and appropriate curves without rushing or causing unintended lead swaps.
purpose: Clarifies rider seat alignment, outside-bend balance, and weight control on curved lines while serving as an optional gymnastic or discipline-specific extension of balanced canter.
safety: Build counter-canter gradually from wide shallow loops on good footing—never force tight counter-canter turns before a horse has strength and balance to carry the outside lead comfortably.
Avoid gripping or tilting to hold a lead by force; if tension builds or the horse swaps early, rebalance calmly on a straight line.

intermediate.overview: Introducing deliberate counter-canter on straight tracks and shallow curves with clear rider alignment and calm three-beat rhythm.

components.title: Understanding counter-canter alignment
components.description: Positioning subtle flexion/bend toward the leading (outside) leg while keeping rider weight centered and hips free—not leaning inward to counterbalance.

components.title: Gradual lines and release
components.description: Riding calm shallow loops off the wall/rail or slight direction changes and transitioning smoothly back to walk or trot before balance unravels.

intermediate.learning: Rides straight lines or shallow counter-canter curves with intermittent inward leaning, tension, breaking to trot, or unintended lead swaps.
intermediate.proficient: Independently prepares and maintains balanced, relaxed counter-canter along straight lines and shallow curves in both directions without rushing, tilting, or forcing the horse's neck.

advanced.overview: Sustaining poised, adjustable counter-canter through deeper curves, loops, and varied transitions while preserving rhythm, comfort, and light, adaptable aids.

components.title: Curve adaptability and timing
components.description: Matching rider weight, rib support, and light outside-lead positioning smoothly as curves deepen or straighten without disturbing three-beat balance.

components.title: Welfare and readiness awareness
components.description: Reading early hindquarter fatigue or cross-canter warning signs and adjusting bend angle, curve radius, or pace thoughtfully.

advanced.learning: Sustains deeper counter-canter loops and transitions with occasional crookedness, stiff outside shoulder, or delayed alignment adjustments.
advanced.proficient: Independently maintains poised, balanced, comfortable counter-canter through deeper loops and curves in both directions, adjusting stride and alignment fluidly on light aids without rushing or tension.

subject: rider
name: Flying Lead Changes
summary: Preparing straight, balanced canter rhythm and delivering clear, light suspension-timed aids to ask for clean flying lead changes in both directions.
purpose: Combines straightness, lead literacy, and stride-phase timing for riders choosing specialized flatwork, pattern, or jumping applications—always prioritizing horse relaxation and physical readiness.
safety: Establish calm, straight simple changes and reliable counter-canter readiness before asking for flying changes; never kick, spur harshly, or throw weight abruptly to provoke a panic swap.
Repeated late hind changes, bucking, pinned ears, or rushing often signal tension, crookedness, conditioning gaps, or back/hock discomfort—step back and evaluate comfort.

advanced.overview: Preparing straightness, balance, and quiet mental focus before asking with light, stride-timed aids for a clean, calm flying change in both directions and adapting thoughtfully to the horse's readiness.

components.title: Preparation and straightness over speed
components.description: Rebalancing the canter squarely between seat and light aids before changing leads—never speeding up or throwing torso weight violently side to side.

components.title: Timing aids to stride suspension
components.description: Delivering calm, coordinated new-lead aids clearly in the preparation/suspension window so front and hind leads change smoothly together.

components.title: Observing quality and adapting cleanly
components.description: Recognizing early anticipation, rushed changes, or late behind immediately and returning quietly to straight counter-canter, simple changes, or comfort checks as needed.

advanced.learning: Prepares and asks for flying changes with occasional rushed approaches, body twisting, unintended early swaps, late hind changes, or rider tension.
advanced.proficient: Independently prepares straight, calm, balanced canter lines, delivers clear, light, stride-timed aids for clean simultaneous flying lead changes in both directions without rushing or harshness, evaluates change quality accurately, and adapts smoothly back to simpler preparation whenever readiness or footing calls for it.

subject: rider
name: Transitions
summary: Preparing and riding smooth, balanced upward, downward, and within-gait transitions—from basic halt–walk–trot changes to accurate marks and direct transitions.
purpose: Develops rider timing, seat preparation, and responsive communication across gaits without pulling, kicking, or rushing.
safety: Prepare transitions progressively rather than abruptly hauling on the reins or kicking with conflicting leg and hand signals.

introductory.overview: Riding calm, safe progressive transitions between halt, walk, and trot with clear preparation and prompt release.

components.title: Preparing before asking
components.description: Checking posture, breathing out, and giving a light cue before escalating calmly if needed. Common mistake: pulling straight back on the reins to stop without using seat/breath, or leaning forward abruptly into trot.

components.title: Prompt release and welfare
components.description: Softening hands and legs the instant the horse responds so transitions stay calm and cooperative rather than tense or resistant.

introductory.learning: Rides halt–walk and walk–trot transitions with coaching; timing may occasionally feel abrupt, delayed, or overly rein-dependent.
introductory.proficient: Independently prepares and rides calm, progressive halt–walk–trot transitions in both directions without abrupt pulling, kicking, or losing basic balance.

intermediate.overview: Smooth progressive upward and downward transitions across halt, walk, trot, and canter—plus halting accurately on a chosen mark.

components.title: Upward and downward preparation
components.description: Using a brief rebalancing moment (half-halt) and straight alignment before asking so the horse shifts weight smoothly instead of hollowing or falling onto the forehand.

components.title: Halt on a mark
components.description: Looking ahead to plan the final strides and halt calmly and accurately at a designated cone, letter, or line without last-second pulling.

intermediate.learning: Rides progressive walk–trot–canter transitions and halts at marks with occasional rushing, lagging, or missed spots.
intermediate.proficient: Independently prepares and rides smooth, balanced progressive upward and downward transitions across halt, walk, trot, and canter, and halts calmly on a chosen mark.

advanced.overview: Coordinating smooth direct transitions (halt–trot, walk–canter, canter–walk, canter–halt) and crisp within-gait adjustments without tension or visible struggle.

components.title: Direct transition preparation
components.description: Using straight alignment, organized core/seat balance, and clear timing so step-up or step-down non-adjacent transitions occur smoothly without leaning forward or hauling backward.

components.title: Within-gait stride control and common errors
components.description: Distinguishing genuine stride lengthening/collection (matching steady tempo) from simply running faster or collapsing onto the forehand. Welfare check: sudden brace or head-tossing during downward changes often signals heavy hand timing or back/dental soreness.

advanced.learning: Practices direct transitions and within-gait changes with intermittent stiffness, bracing hands, or hurried tempo.
advanced.proficient: Independently prepares and rides balanced direct transitions and clear within-gait stride adjustments in both directions with quiet, coordinated aids, straight rider alignment, and soft prompt release.

exercises.title: Breath-First Preparation Through Walk and Trot
exercises.summary: Practice halt-to-walk, walk-to-trot, and gentle downward returns by organizing your posture and exhale one stride ahead before lightly adding leg or soft rein feel—releasing pressure immediately as the new gait begins.
exercises.whatToNotice: Observe whether transitions unfold smoothly without sudden head-up reactions or lagging delays caused by conflicting hand and leg signals.

exercises.title: Spot-On Marks and Smooth Direct Transitions
exercises.summary: Pick a visual arena landmark such as a cone or rail post and prepare three strides early so halt or gait shifts happen cleanly right beside the mark—progressing for advanced pairs into balanced direct transitions (halt-to-trot or walk-to-canter) with minimal visible effort.
exercises.whatToNotice: Notice whether preparing earlier lets you use half the rein or leg intensity while getting smoother, straighter responses.

commonDifficulties.issue: Pulling backward while squeezing legs simultaneously
commonDifficulties.guidance: Contradictory cues trap the horse between go and stop. Separate your timing clearly: prepare posture first, ask with lightest clear signal, then immediately follow the new stride.

commonDifficulties.issue: Surprising the horse right on the cone without warning
commonDifficulties.guidance: Last-second abrupt halts dump weight onto the shoulders. Whisper a tiny check two strides ahead so balance shifts smoothly underneath you.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: The quality of every transition lives in the three preparation strides before it happens.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Avoid abrupt yanking downward halts or forceful kicking upward; check dental, back, and saddle comfort if downward transitions reliably prompt head tossing.

subject: rider
name: Half-Halt (Rebalancing)
summary: Using a brief, coordinated rebalancing request to gather the horse's attention and balance before a turn, figure, or transition.
purpose: Allows the rider to shift balance back from the forehand and prepare the horse smoothly without breaking gait or pulling continuously.
safety: Always release promptly after the rebalancing moment; never hold continuous backward pressure.

intermediate.overview: Coordinating seat, core, leg, and brief soft rein timing to gather the horse's attention and rebalance before turns or transitions—whether riding on elastic contact or a light drape.

components.title: Coordinated timing and immediate release
components.description: Organizing posture and core briefly, maintaining gentle forward support with the legs, closing fingers for a fraction of a stride (or lifting gentle feel on a draped rein), and softening instantly as the stride checks and settles.

components.title: Common mistakes and welfare check
components.description: Holding backward pressure across multiple strides turns a half-halt into a continuous brake and teaches the horse to lean or hollow. Verify breath remains relaxed and jaw stays soft after every rebalancing cue.

intermediate.learning: Practices half-halt timing with coaching; pressure sometimes lingers past release or unintentionally stalls forward rhythm.
intermediate.proficient: Independently uses subtle, momentary rebalancing requests (seat, leg, and soft timely release) before turns and transitions without breaking gait rhythm or holding continuous backward pressure.

exercises.title: Quiet Seat-Core Gather Before a Line Change
exercises.summary: Riding walk or trot on either elastic contact or a gentle drape, pause two strides before a corner or transition: grow momentarily taller through your torso, close legs lightly like an attentive hug, give a brief half-second elastic check on the reins, and immediately yield hands forward again.
exercises.whatToNotice: Did the horse’s attention return and stride balance softly for a beat without pulling the chin back—and did your fingers truly release within one beat?

exercises.title: Chaining Half-Halts to Soften Long Strides
exercises.summary: When a horse leans onto the forehand along a long line or gentle downgrade, offer two or three light spaced breath-and-seat checks with full yields between them rather than one long steady pull.
exercises.whatToNotice: Notice how brief pulsed releases keep the jaw mobile and receptive, whereas holding tension longer than one stride invites leaning back against you.

commonDifficulties.issue: Holding the rein check continuously instead of releasing
commonDifficulties.guidance: A half-halt without a prompt yield is simply backward pulling. Exaggerate letting your fingers soften forward on the very next beat until timing becomes automatic.

commonDifficulties.issue: Dropping forward or pinching knees during the core brace
commonDifficulties.guidance: Collapsing at the waist throws weight onto the shoulders you were trying to lighten. Think of lengthening quietly up through the crown of your head and exhaling.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Think of a half-halt as tapping a shoulder to say "listen, next curve ahead"—never grabbing a brake lever.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Never pull backward while driving forward aggressively; a balanced half-halt stays under one second and preserves free breath and soft jaw.

subject: rider
name: Steering & Navigation
summary: Guiding a horse accurately along straight lines, circles, turns, and marker patterns with appropriate bend, rhythm, and look-ahead.
purpose: Unifies arena geometry and pattern navigation into one core steering ability across walk, trot, and canter.
safety: Look well ahead around turns to protect arena/trail spacing, align markers generously for the gait, and keep turning radius safe for footing and speed.

introductory.overview: Guiding straight lines away from walls, recognizable large circles (e.g., ~20 m), turns, and simple cone patterns at walk with clear look-ahead.

components.title: Look-ahead and guiding the shoulders
components.description: Turning your eyes and shoulders gently toward the next point and pairing light opening rein feel with outside leg/rein awareness instead of dragging the horse's nose sharply sideways with one rein.

components.title: Lines, generous circles, and common mistakes
components.description: Maintaining steady track off the rail, riding rounded balanced arcs, and keeping walk energy steady without stalling mid-turn.

introductory.learning: Steers straight lines and walk patterns with occasional shoulder drift toward the rail, sharp corner cutting, or leaning inward.
introductory.proficient: Independently steers balanced straight lines, recognizable generous arcs (such as ~20 m circles), turns, and simple marker paths at walk with clear look-ahead and safe spacing.

intermediate.overview: Riding accurate figures and cone/serpentine patterns at trot with smooth bend changes, consistent rhythm, and timely rider preparation.

components.title: Early bend transitions between arcs
components.description: Straightening smoothly across change-of-direction lines before establishing the new arc so trot rhythm stays steady and neither shoulder bulges outward.

intermediate.learning: Rides trot figures and patterns with late aid transitions, drifted circles, or rushed tempo around tighter turns.
intermediate.proficient: Independently guides accurate lines, circles, serpentines, and marker patterns at trot with consistent tempo, early bend transitions, and balanced posture.

advanced.overview: Navigating complex figures and marker patterns at canter with planned pace control, balanced geometry, and calm lead choices.

components.title: Canter path planning and lead awareness
components.description: Organizing balanced canter speed ahead of turns and selecting purposeful simple transitions, flying changes, or deliberate counter-canter suited to the horse's training.

advanced.learning: Navigates canter patterns with intermittent wide turns, rushed arcs, or late lead management.
advanced.proficient: Independently rides varied canter figures and patterns with poised rider balance, accurate geometry, sound speed judgment, and calm, deliberate lead management.

exercises.title: Eyes Ahead and Shoulder-Led Lines Away From the Rail
exercises.summary: Step a horse’s width off the arena wall at walk to check genuine steering away from rail support. Turn your eyes and torso clearly toward each cone or target around large circles and straight lines, inviting shoulders around gently with aligned legs rather than yanking the nose sideways.
exercises.whatToNotice: Check whether your eyes lock down at the horse’s ears—looking two turns ahead keeps paths smooth and shoulders balanced.

exercises.title: Changing Bend Smoothly Through Serpentines and Patterns
exercises.summary: At trot—and canter for advanced pairs—weave wide serpentines, figure-eights, or open cone corridors while briefly straightening the horse for two clear strides between every curve before re-aligning seat, shoulders, and legs for the new bend.
exercises.whatToNotice: Notice how much cleaner turns feel when your outside rein and thigh guide shoulder drift rather than dragging the inside rein toward your hip.

commonDifficulties.issue: Pulling the inside rein across the withers to steer
commonDifficulties.guidance: Crossing your hand over the neck bends the spine crookedly and lets the outside shoulder bulge out. Open space softly toward the turn direction and frame the outside shoulder calmly.

commonDifficulties.issue: Forging steep hairpin bends at faster gaits
commonDifficulties.guidance: Tight high-speed turns overload ankles and balance. Match circle radius generously to gait speed and footing traction.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Ride the line with your eyes, chest, and hips first—hands only guide where the horse’s body was already invited.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Maintain safe arena/trail passing distances, inspect turns for slickness, and remember uneven steering often reflects rider crookedness or one-sided discomfort.

subject: rider
name: Turn on the Forehand
summary: Guiding a reasonably prepared horse to step its hindquarters laterally around a relatively steady forehand.
purpose: Develops independent hindquarter control for opening space, gate alignment, and early lateral coordination.
safety: Avoid pulling the horse backward or trapping its mouth while asking for sideways steps.

introductory.overview: From halt or very slow walk, guiding partial or half turns (e.g., ~90–180°) on the forehand cleanly in both directions with calm timing and release.

components.title: Balanced seat and timed leg release
components.description: Sitting upright over both seat bones without collapsing onto the inside hip, positioning slightly back with one leg to ask the hindquarters over while soft reins invite stillness ahead without clamping backward.

introductory.learning: Guides turns on the forehand with occasional uneven crossing, stiff hips, or heavy rein pressure that backs the horse up.
introductory.proficient: Independently prepares from halt or slow walk and guides smooth, partial-to-half turns on the forehand in both directions using balanced posture, soft non-restrictive reins, and prompt leg release.

intermediate.overview: Guiding sustained or full turns on the forehand in both directions with minimal pivot drift, even rhythm, and seamless transitions in and out of walk.

components.title: Preventing backward drift and timing walk exits
components.description: Balancing soft forward allowance with clear lateral leg aids so each hind step tracks cleanly around a quiet front pivot before walking smoothly straight out—checking hock/hip ease rather than nagging with continuous heel kicks.

intermediate.learning: Refines longer turns on the forehand and walk exits with occasional backward steps, pivot drift, or tense timing.
intermediate.proficient: Independently coordinates clean, rhythmic turns on the forehand in both directions using subtle forward-allowing hands and timed leg cues so the forehand stays steady, steps flow smoothly, and walk exits stay poised.

exercises.title: Opening the Door for a Few Hind Steps
exercises.summary: From a settled halt or very slow walk on flat ground, sit evenly over both seat bones with soft non-pulling hands, shift one leg gently behind the girth to invite one or two calm hindquarter steps sideways around a relatively steady front end, and immediately relax back to neutral.
exercises.whatToNotice: Notice whether your upper body collapses sideways—staying upright over the pivot keeps front feet balanced while hind legs cross freely.

exercises.title: Clean Rhythm and Seamless Walk Exits
exercises.summary: Guide smooth 180° or full 360° forehand turns in both directions while maintaining light directional control over the shoulders, finishing with a clean step directly into a straight working walk.
exercises.whatToNotice: Check whether both sides feel equally fluid without clamping on the mouth or letting the horse step backward out of the turn.

commonDifficulties.issue: Pulling back on both reins to hold the front feet still
commonDifficulties.guidance: Continuous rein pressure makes the horse back up or freeze tightly. Offer only a soft steadying reminder, release between crossing steps, and let forward flow stay available.

commonDifficulties.issue: Sliding your leg abruptly way back to the flank
commonDifficulties.guidance: Over-reaching behind destabilizes your seat. Ask softly slightly behind the girth and wait calmly a moment for the horse to organize.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Hold space gently in front with lightness rather than locking the mouth—then the hindquarters step smoothly around.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Practice only short turns in each direction on non-slippery ground and check saddle fit and stifle/hock comfort if stiff resistance repeats.

subject: rider
name: Turn on the Haunches
summary: Guiding a reasonably prepared horse from walk to step its forehand smoothly around steadier hindquarters with clarity, balance, and discipline-neutral coordination.
purpose: Builds independent shoulder responsiveness, forward turning balance, and practical precision for gates, trail turns, working horsemanship, and coordinated lateral development.
safety: Maintain calm forward walk rhythm into every turn on safe, non-slippery footing—never wrench the forehand sideways with the inside rein or twist the horse abruptly onto a stuck hind leg.
Adjust turning radius to the horse's conditioning, conformation, and ground conditions rather than chasing tight pivots prematurely.

introductory.overview: Building foundational understanding and calm coordination: inviting the forehand smoothly around steadier hindquarters on a generous walk arc in both directions without hauling the inside rein or pushing backward.

components.title: Understanding forward walk flow around the hindquarters
components.description: Looking softly through the intended arc and supporting forward walk rhythm rather than halting dead first or letting steps collapse into backward evasion.

components.title: Clear shoulder guidance vs. inside-rein pulling
components.description: Using balanced upper-body direction, clear outside-shoulder/neck guidance suited to your bridle/discipline, and calm seat clarity rather than hauling the horse's nose inward toward your knee.

components.title: Common mistakes and footing awareness
components.description: Notice if the hindquarters swing outward instead of staying relatively centered, or if the horse stalls into backing; reset politely onto a straight walk rather than forcing tighter turns on uneven ground.

introductory.learning: Guides generous walk turns around the hindquarters with occasional uneven rhythm, wide drifting, backward steps, or heavy reliance on inside rein pressure.
introductory.proficient: Independently prepares from calm walk and guides smooth, rhythmic, generous turns of the forehand around steadier hindquarters in both directions using clear, non-pulling shoulder aids without spinning or backing.

intermediate.overview: Developing higher precision, balanced preparation, active four-beat rhythm, and adaptability across practical contexts and disciplines (gates, trails, open work, or arena turns).

components.title: Preparation and coordinated precision
components.description: Using subtle rebalancing (half-halt) and balanced weight over both seat bones before initiating the turn so the horse steps lightly around steadier hindquarters in steady rhythm and exits cleanly onto the chosen line.

components.title: Discipline-neutral adaptability and footing judgment
components.description: Adapting turning radius, rein feel (elastic two-hand contact or light draped/neck rein), and alignment to suit the horse's conformation, ground traction, and riding context—without mandating fixed degree counts or competition-style collection.

components.title: Welfare awareness and common errors
components.description: Respecting subtle left/right stiffness and hock comfort; stopping short or widening the arc if stepping loses pure walk rhythm or causes neck brace.

intermediate.learning: Guides coordinated, smaller-radius turns around the hindquarters with intermittent loss of walk beat, stiff neck alignment, slightly rushed exits, or uneven directional control.
intermediate.proficient: Independently prepares, coordinates, and adapts smooth, accurate turns around steadier hindquarters in both directions across suitable contexts and riding styles—maintaining clear walk rhythm, comfortable alignment, sound footing judgment, and clean straight exits.

exercises.title: Turning Shoulders Smoothly on a Generous Walk Arc
exercises.summary: Walking actively forward on good footing, gather attention softly with posture and a brief half-halt, then look smoothly toward the turn direction, bring your chest around while maintaining light forward walk stepping, and carry the shoulders politely across a generous arc before riding straight out.
exercises.whatToNotice: Does the horse keep stepping forward with every beat around the arc, or did heavy inside rein pull stop the hind legs and stall the turn?

exercises.title: Compact Walk Turn Through Practical Angles
exercises.summary: Apply smooth shoulder-guiding coordination through narrower gate turns, trail switchbacks, or compact arena turns in both directions—maintaining even walk rhythm and balanced outside-aid framing adapted to your discipline.
exercises.whatToNotice: Check whether outside leg and seat softly regulate hind-leg activity so the pivot stays rhythmic rather than twisting awkwardly on a planted hind foot.

commonDifficulties.issue: Pulling the inside rein backward toward your hip
commonDifficulties.guidance: Directing backward forces the neck sideways while the shoulder pops outward. Steer with open chest turn, supporting outside rein boundary, and forward seat energy.

commonDifficulties.issue: Chasing fast tight spins prematurely
commonDifficulties.guidance: Tight pivots before strength and rhythm develop torque hind joints harshly. Keep turns wide and active in clear walk rhythm.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Forward walk rhythm is the engine of every turn on the haunches—lose the walk beat and you lose balance.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Never wrench turns on deep, sticky, or slick ground; adapt arc tightness thoughtfully to horse conformation, fitness, and joint health.

subject: rider
name: Rein Back
aliases: Back through an L or corridor
summary: Guiding a reasonably prepared horse to step calmly backward in a diagonal two-beat pattern—on straight lines or through patterns like an L or corridor.
purpose: Improves responsiveness, straightness, and practical maneuvering for gates, tight spaces, and trail patterns.
safety: Maintain soft, clear requests and yield hands promptly forward once steps are offered—never see-saw, pull continuously, or force backward into bracing.
Always verify clear space behind you and check tack/back/hock comfort if the horse repeatedly throws its head or refuses.

intermediate.overview: Guiding smooth, straight diagonal backward lines in open space—or cleanly through optional corridors/L-patterns if practiced—then halting or walking on smoothly.

components.title: Keeping straightness and rhythm without force
components.description: Using quiet leg channels to steady drifting hips while keeping light elastic reins rather than clamping backward. Common mistake: pulling harder when a horse stalls or rushes sideways instead of walking calmly forward to reset.

intermediate.learning: Guides multi-step straight backing or optional corridor lines with intermittent hip drift, rushed steps, or delayed rein softening.
intermediate.proficient: Independently asks for calm, straight backward steps on open lines (and through optional gates, corridors, or L patterns where practiced) with light guiding legs, non-forceful rein feel, and smooth forward departures.

advanced.overview: Guiding adaptable straight and curved backing alignments, practical obstacle backing, and smooth transitions between rein-back and walk or trot.

components.title: Adjustable alignment and composed walk/trot departures
components.description: Directing subtle shoulder and hip adjustments mid-rein-back along curves, slopes, or practical trail obstacles and riding smooth calm departures into walk or trot without rushing or hollowing (without needing harsh direct canter leaps from rein-back).

advanced.learning: Manages curved backing lines, technical obstacles, or walk/trot departures with occasional crookedness or brief rush out of halt.
advanced.proficient: Independently adjusts straight and curved rein-back lines across varied practical tasks and steps smoothly into balanced walk or trot on light cue without brace or harshness.

introductory.overview: Preparing a calm halt on flat open ground and asking cleanly for 1–3 quiet backward steps with instant release forward.

components.title: Halt preparation, posture, and immediate release
components.description: Stopping calmly and evenly first, checking clear space behind, keeping thighs relaxed so you do not grip tight against the backward invite, offering soft brief backward feel with seat/reins/legs, and softening forward as soon as the horse shifts weight back or takes 1–3 quiet steps.

introductory.learning: Asks for a step or two back with reminders not to lean far back, clench knees, or keep pulling after the horse starts backing.
introductory.proficient: Independently prepares a calm halt on flat open ground, keeps neutral seat clearance, asks softly for 1–3 quiet backward steps, and releases cleanly forward into halt or walk.

exercises.title: One Calm Step at a Time
exercises.summary: Verify open space behind you, then begin from a balanced, quiet halt. Ask lightly for a single backward step with unclamped legs, release your aids immediately, and allow the horse to settle before repeating.
exercises.whatToNotice: Does the horse understand the request without bracing, rushing, or hollowing its back—and did your hands soften forward the moment the weight shifted?

exercises.title: Straight Line, Quiet Reset Forward
exercises.summary: From a square halt on flat open footing, invite a few balanced backward steps while keeping even leg channels to discourage drifting hips. Pause softly without chasing fixed step counts, then walk smoothly forward so backing stays willing.
exercises.whatToNotice: Notice whether you guide drifting hindquarters subtly with aligned seat and legs instead of fixing crookedness by pulling harder on one rein.

commonDifficulties.issue: Maintaining rein tension after the horse begins stepping back
commonDifficulties.guidance: Holding pressure once the horse tries rewards rushing or bracing. Release promptly forward on the earliest backward weight shift.

commonDifficulties.issue: Leaning back or pinching thighs during the request
commonDifficulties.guidance: Clamping knees and driving seat weight heavily downward often blocks the horse's back. Stay centered over your seat bones and walk forward to reset if tension builds.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: The release is part of the lesson, not simply the end of it.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Persistent resistance can indicate discomfort or confusion—simplify to a relaxed walk forward and check saddle, dental, back, and hock comfort before asking again.

subject: rider
name: Sidepass
summary: Guiding a reasonably prepared horse to step directly sideways with even crossing of front and hind legs, in open space or over a ground rail.
purpose: Provides exact lateral positioning for gates, obstacles, and independent control of shoulders and hips.
safety: If riding over an optional ground pole, use a heavy stable pole on even footing and allow clear alignment so the horse does not tangle a hoof.

intermediate.overview: Guiding straight sideways steps cleanly in both directions—in open space, beside a fence/gate, or optionally aligned over a ground rail.

components.title: Balanced sideways coordination
components.description: Staying centered over the spine while coordinating subtle forward-checking reins and sideways-inviting leg pressure, shifting quietly if shoulders or hips lag ahead/behind.

components.title: Optional rail alignment and common mistakes
components.description: When practiced over an optional ground pole, aligning parallel and pausing briefly if steps hurry. Avoid leaning way off the horse's side or kicking repeatedly against stiff confusion.

intermediate.learning: Guides sideways steps with occasional forward/backward leak, body twisting, or uneven shoulder-to-hip alignment.
intermediate.proficient: Independently guides calm, straight sideways steps in both directions—in open space, at a gate, or optionally over a ground rail—using balanced posture and clear, non-rushed aids.

subject: rider
name: Leg Yield
summary: Guiding a reasonably prepared horse forward and sideways simultaneously at walk or trot with a straight body or slight flexion away from the direction of travel.
purpose: Teaches the rider to coordinate forward and lateral requests without losing rhythm, balance, or straightness.
safety: Avoid pulling backward on the reins while asking for sideways movement; ensure clear arena space.

intermediate.overview: Coordinating clear walk-first and trot leg yields in both directions while preserving steady forward flow and balanced alignment.

components.title: Inside leg to outside rein coordination
components.description: Establishing solid sideways feel at walk first, guiding the horse forward and sideways along diagonal tracks with soft outside-rein containment and gentle inside-leg timing rather than pulling the head sideways with the inside rein.

intermediate.learning: Rides leg yield at walk or trot with inconsistent angle, rushed tempo, or shoulders racing ahead of the hips.
intermediate.proficient: Independently guides balanced, rhythmic leg yields in both directions at walk and trot, balancing forward flow against outside support and returning smoothly to straight lines.

exercises.title: Walk Diagonal Yield Off the Quarterline
exercises.summary: At an active working walk along an inside line parallel to the fence, keep your torso tall facing straight ahead toward the distant wall while applying soft side-moving leg on one side and calming outside boundary—inviting forward-and-sideways steps evenly back toward the rail.
exercises.whatToNotice: Notice whether the horse’s shoulders stay cleanly ahead of or aligned with the hips rather than trailing the haunches behind or crossing crookedly.

exercises.title: Trot Leg Yield Preserving Forward Cadence
exercises.summary: Once walk yields stay smooth and soft in both directions, introduce short, well-balanced leg yields at a comfortable trot along diagonal paths, keeping slight steady flexion away from travel without pulling back on the mouth.
exercises.whatToNotice: Check whether trot tempo stays steady and rhythmic through each sideways step—rushing fast or stalling flat signals your aids pushed too abruptly.

commonDifficulties.issue: Hips trailing way behind while the horse leans crookedly forward
commonDifficulties.guidance: If only the shoulder moves sideways, keep your guiding leg smoothly near the barrel while outside rein regulates forward escape—or step briefly back to walk until balanced.

commonDifficulties.issue: Bending the horse too far toward the travel direction
commonDifficulties.guidance: True leg yield maintains a straight spine with only subtle poll softening away from direction; excessive neck bend blocks shoulder crossing.

learningGuide.trainerInsight: Think forward first, sideways second—the horse must still have room ahead to step gracefully across.
learningGuide.welfareNote: Keep diagonal yields brief and even both ways; persistent stiffness one side often highlights saddle asymmetry, stifle tenderness, or rib tension.

subject: rider
name: Shoulder-In
summary: Guiding a horse along a straight line with the shoulders brought slightly inward and a slight, even bend away from the direction of travel.
purpose: Develops rider feel for bend, straightness, and engagement of the inside hind leg as a foundation for advanced lateral work.
safety: Build from shallow angles and short sections; never force neck bend with the reins.

intermediate.overview: Establishing clear shoulder-fore or shallow shoulder-in at walk in both directions (with optional brief trot exploration) before returning straight.

components.title: Guiding shoulders off the track without neck-bending only
components.description: Setting a mild uniform bend off a turn or corner, keeping your own shoulders parallel to the horse's shoulders, and riding forward along the track rather than curling only the neck inward while the haunches drift out.

intermediate.learning: Positions shoulders inward at walk with inconsistent track, crooked rider shoulders, or neck-only bend.
intermediate.proficient: Independently rides a recognizable, functional shoulder-fore or shoulder-in at walk in both directions using balanced seat, leg, and half-halt timing to hold the line smoothly before straightening. Trot proficiency is not required.

advanced.overview: Sustaining balanced, uniform shoulder-in at trot along full lines in both directions and linking cleanly into other figures or lateral work.

components.title: Sustained trot balance, clarity, and physical ease
components.description: Coordinating outside half-halts and inside seat/leg timing to maintain even three-track spacing and tempo without forcing steep angles or tension—keeping segments sensible for the horse's strength.

advanced.learning: Sustains trot shoulder-in with intermittent flattening, falling sideways, or rushed rhythm during transitions back to straight.
advanced.proficient: Independently rides sustained, rhythmic shoulder-in at trot along full lines in both directions using balanced alignment and soft, responsive timing through clear entries and straight exits.

subject: rider
name: Travers (Haunches-In)
summary: Guiding a reasonably prepared horse along a straight line at walk or trot with slight inward bend (in the direction of travel), keeping the forehand on the track while carrying the hindquarters slightly inward.
purpose: Advances rider coordination, independent seat control, and feel for lateral collection.
safety: Avoid hauling the head sharply inward or forcing steep angles on stiff or tired horses; keep segments brief and prioritize smooth rhythm.

advanced.overview: Guiding smooth travers (haunches-in) in both directions at walk and trot using subtle seat-hip angle and true inward bend.

components.title: Seat positioning and true inward bend
components.description: Mirroring the movement softly in your pelvis while guarding the outside shoulder on the track and asking the hindquarters slightly inward (a shallow ~30° track angle)—catching common mistakes like dropping onto the inside seat bone or pulling inside rein sharply.

advanced.learning: Practices travers at walk or trot with intermittent forehand drift off the track, twisted rider hips, or over-bent neck.
advanced.proficient: Independently guides balanced travers in both directions at walk and trot using true slight inward bend, attentive forehand track control, clear outside-leg timing, and steady rhythm.

subject: rider
name: Terrain & Obstacle Negotiation
summary: Guiding a horse safely and confidently across ground poles, bridges, tarps, water crossings, slopes, and varied terrain.
purpose: Builds balanced rider posture, clear forward support, and sound judgment across unfamiliar footing and environmental challenges.
safety: Evaluate footing grip, bridge decking, water depth/currents, overhead clearance, and hidden holes before committing across any obstacle or slope.
Never snag the horse's mouth for balance while climbing, stepping onto bridges/drops, or balancing through mud—use crest support or mane/strap when climbing steep slopes.

introductory.overview: Riding calmly across straightforward obstacles (ground poles, low bridges, tarps, shallow puddles, gentle grades) at walk with free head balance.

components.title: Allowing balance and look-time at walk
components.description: Keeping centered weight on gentle slopes, releasing forward hand reach so the horse can drop its head to look and balance over poles or bridges, and rewarding calm forward steps rather than kicking against curiosity.

introductory.learning: Crosses simple obstacles and gentle grades at walk with occasional pinched heels, tight reins over poles, or tipped-forward posture.
introductory.proficient: Independently approaches and rides calmly over straightforward ground obstacles, shallow water, and gentle slopes at walk with independent seat balance, non-restrictive reins, and straight intent.

intermediate.overview: Balancing uphill/downhill slopes, natural water crossings, uneven ground, and appropriate trot pole or safe terrain lines thoughtfully.

components.title: Slope weight placement and trot-line adjustment
components.description: Inclining shoulders quietly over your center of mass uphill (giving crest/mane freedom) and staying stacked upright without bracing backward into the cantle downhill, plus adapting light seat/two-point smoothly over trot poles or uneven earth.

intermediate.learning: Rides steeper slopes, natural water, or trot lines with occasional forward pitching, hand snagging, or rushed entry.
intermediate.proficient: Independently manages uphill/downhill balance, natural water crossings, uneven terrain, and appropriate trot obstacle lines safely with elastic hand follow and composed pacing.

advanced.overview: Navigating complex outdoor terrain and appropriate canter lines while exercising disciplined judgment about speed, footing, and when to walk.

components.title: Footing awareness and responsible pace judgment
components.description: Adjusting stride length cleanly at canter over appropriate ground work or safe open trails, while promptly down-transitioning whenever blind turns, slick turf, slick rock, deep mud, or steep drops make slower careful footing safer.

advanced.learning: Handles varied terrain combinations or canter tracks with occasional late speed adjustments before slick or technical transitions.
advanced.proficient: Independently navigates complex terrain and appropriate canter lines with secure athletic balance, stride awareness, and sound judgment on when slower pacing protects horse and rider.

subject: rider
name: Object Handling
summary: Managing gates and handling, carrying, moving, or placing objects (such as gates, bells, mail, ropes, rings, or poles) while mounted.
purpose: Integrates calm standing, one-handed control, and precise horse positioning for trail riding, ranch work, and working equitation.
safety: Keep steady control of gates so they do not swing into horse or rider; be ready to release an object and ride safely if the horse spooks.
Gates and similar fixed latch tasks are handled at halt/walk—never require unsafe gaits for an object.

introductory.overview: Fundamental object handling at halt or walk (such as picking up, carrying, or placing simple objects, ringing a bell, or basic assisted gate work).

components.title: One-handed balance at halt and walk
components.description: Reaching, holding, or placing an object smoothly without pulling on the reins or losing seat balance.

introductory.learning: Handles simple objects at halt or walk with occasional horse drift, fumbled rein transfers, or pauses.
introductory.proficient: Independently handles, carries, and places simple objects calmly at halt or walk while maintaining balanced posture and steady horse control.

intermediate.overview: Coordinated handling—such as independently opening, passing through, and closing a gate cleanly, or carrying/exchanging objects at trot where appropriate.

components.title: Gate management
components.description: Positioning beside the latch, controlling the gate through the pass-through, and latching calmly at halt/walk.

components.title: Trot object coordination
components.description: Carrying or placing appropriate objects smoothly at trot without losing rhythm or line.

intermediate.learning: Opens/closes gates or carries objects at trot with occasional repositioning, gate-swing, or tempo changes.
intermediate.proficient: Independently manages gates cleanly from halt/walk and performs coordinated object handling (including trot applications where appropriate) with calm one-handed control.

advanced.overview: Managing complex object interactions—including accurate handling at canter where appropriate—with poised one-handed seat/leg control.

components.title: Independent one-handed balance at speed
components.description: Maintaining upright core and clear seat/leg direction without drifting left/right or jerking the spare rein hand while picking up, maneuvering, or placing objects cleanly at canter where appropriate and safe.

advanced.learning: Practices complex or canter object tasks with intermittent leaning, crooked line drift, or unsteady spare hand.
advanced.proficient: Independently carries out complex object-handling tasks—including accurate handling at canter where appropriate—using steady one-handed balance, subtle seat/leg guidance, and safe release timing.
